articles.title: Insecure attachment linked to reduced well-being in bisexual young adults
articles.summary: A recent study tracking emerging adult bisexual women in Chile found that insecure attachment styles predict lower future well-being, highlighting the need to look beyond psychological distress when evaluating mental health.

articles.title: People project a specific racial identity onto artificial intelligence, study finds
articles.summary: Does AI have a race? In people’s minds, it often does. Across studies in the U.S., Japan, and India, participants tended to associate faceless AI systems with Whiteness.

articles.title: Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain
articles.summary: A surprising discovery suggests that some early signs of Alzheimer’s disease may begin outside the brain. Using miniature laboratory systems made from human cells, scientists found that genetic mutations associated with inherited Alzheimer’s can disrupt nerve-to-muscle connections without any involvement from the brain or spinal cord. This could help explain why some patients experience changes in balance, walking, and coordination long before memory problems develop.

articles.title: Greater male variability may help explain persistent gender gaps in hiring, study suggests
articles.summary: Men and women can earn the same average score on a job test and still face unequal hiring odds. A simulation study suggests that when employers screen out most applicants, wider spread in men’s scores tilts hiring toward men.

articles.title: Autistic individuals show altered white matter in long-range brain pathways
articles.summary: Pooling data from 66 brain imaging studies, researchers found that autistic individuals showed differences in white matter microstructure across many of the brain’s major pathways, particularly long-range tracts linking distant regions.

articles.title: The best conversations may follow a hidden mathematical rhythm called pink noise, according to new psychology research
articles.summary: Enjoyable conversations tend not to stay in perfect agreement. A study of thousands of chats found that those with a stronger “pink noise” pattern of drifting apart and coming back together were rated as more enjoyable.

articles.title: Frontiers: A Roundtable Discussion on the I-Frame vs. S-Frame Debate
articles.summary: Applied behavioral scientists believe their work can influence people’s lives for the better. But what is the most effective way to make that happen? Is it through interventions focused on influencing individual behavior while maintaining freedom of choice? Is it by changing policies and laws, and thereby the systems, that individuals operate within? Is it a combination of the two? Is the distinction between an individual- or systems-focus a helpful one? Or, is the world too messy and complex? How should applied behavioral scientists navigate the financial and political influences on the work

articles.title: Even occasional marijuana use linked to 40% higher odds of stroke
articles.summary: New research involving more than 440,000 Americans links cannabis use to increased cardiovascular risk, with occasional users showing 40% higher odds of reporting a history of stroke. The findings suggest that even infrequent marijuana use may warrant concern, although researchers have not established that cannabis directly causes strokes or heart disease.

articles.title: Obesity linked to up to 27% lower risk of death in dementia
articles.summary: A surprising study of more than 4,500 older adults found that people who were overweight or obese when diagnosed with dementia had a 16% to 27% lower risk of death than those at a normal weight. Researchers suspect that extra energy and muscle reserves may help patients survive the disease's toll on the body, although the reason for the survival advantage remains unclear.

articles.title: Scientists finally discover why we learn to love bitter coffee
articles.summary: Scientists have uncovered a hidden gut-to-brain dopamine pathway that helps explain why bitter coffee and other initially unpleasant flavors can become favorites over time. The discovery reveals how the brain learns to crave certain foods and could eventually lead to new ways of reshaping eating habits and food preferences.

articles.title: Auditable Human-Agent Teams for Autonomous X-ray Experimentation
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.12933v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Closed-loop autonomous experimentation can accelerate scientific discovery, but implementation effort limits accessibility. Agentic systems may lower this barrier, although sustained operation on physical instruments remains largely unexplored. Here, using coding-agent infrastructure grounded in validated scientific methods, we demonstrate autonomous synchrotron X-ray experiments on nanoparticle superlattices under evolving, human-defined objectives. Complete human-agent and agent-agent transcripts enable an audit that reconstructs decision prove

articles.title: Train on prefill, monitor at decode: Using sparse autoencoders for topic monitoring
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.12935v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Topic monitoring is the task of labelling the topic of each token in a model's response during generation. Activation-based monitors that run at generation time have so far been trained to detect harmful content and are limited to two or three classes. We introduce TopicScope, a framework for training causal topic classifiers on SAE features that assign a topic to every token, so that the label can change partway through a response. We train three detector architectures on synthetic multi-topic conversations covering seven topics. Across Gemma-3
